result:
The proposed answer of 1/3 is not justified, and I think it is likely wrong.

The trivial upper bound is λ ≤ n/3, since each P₃ uses 3 vertices, so c ≤ 1/3. The solution's construction (inserting a degree-3 vertex into every face of a triangulation H on k vertices) also gives only λ ≤ k ≈ n/3, which is the same as the trivial bound. So that construction shows nothing new, and the solution never proves a lower bound matching 1/3. It claims λ "probably" equals k without checking this.

Saying c = 1/3 would mean every plane triangulation has an almost perfect P₃-packing. The problem asks for an "exact value" of a constant, which suggests a nontrivial extremal construction pushing c strictly below 1/3. The solution itself says it is unsure and recalls "2n/7" as a possibility. I believe the true constant is below 1/3, but I could not derive it here, so this rejection rests on that expectation and not on an explicit counterexample.

VERDICT: REJECT
